title: Does my state follow the federal trench rule? States where federal OSHA's 5 ft trench rule applies to private crews
topic: Trench and excavation rules: which states follow federal OSHA
text: Where a state has no state OSHA plan for private employers, federal OSHA covers private construction crews and its trench rule applies with no state difference: a protective system (sloping, benching, shoring or a trench box / shield) in an excavation 5 ft or deeper unless it is entirely in stable rock, and in a shallower one when the competent person sees signs of a possible cave-in (29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)). Use only the line for the job's state. Federal rule, no state OSHA plan (OSHA list of State Plans): Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Dakota, Texas, West Virginia, Wisconsin. Federal rule for private crews, state plan for public employees only: Connecticut, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York. In these states there is no separate state trench depth rule for private crews in the library. The other 21 states run their own plan for private crews (see the state-plan list). The competent person decides what protection a trench gets.
source: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1); OSHA State Plans list (osha.gov/stateplans); app state table checked 2026-11-19
edition: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P as in effect Nov 2026; OSHA State Plans list read 2026-11-20
note: Replaces the 24 one-state cards sp-<st>-trench-1 (AL AR CO DE DC FL GA ID KS LA MS MO MT NE NH ND OH OK PA RI SD TX WV WI) that all said the same thing; CT IL ME MA NJ NY from sp-<st>-who-1.

title: State OSHA plans and the trench rule: which plan states follow federal 5 ft, which differ, which are not checked
topic: Trench and excavation rules: which states follow federal OSHA
text: Twenty-one states run their own OSHA plan for private construction crews. A plan must be at least as protective as federal OSHA (protection from 5 ft, 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)) and may be stricter, so name the plan as the source. Use only the line for the job's state. As checked by 2026-11-20. The plan adopts the federal excavation rule, so 5 ft: Alaska, Arizona (R20-5-601), Kentucky (803 KAR 2:415), Minnesota (MNOSHA trenching fact sheet: no state difference), Nevada, New Mexico (11.5.3.9 NMAC), Tennessee, Utah (R614-1-4), Indiana (620 IAC 1-1-30 items 7 and 18 adopt 29 CFR 1926.650-652, in force March 5, 1990, with no Indiana depth or permit of its own; OSHA's page lists an Indiana excavation standard that was not identified, not confirmed: ask IOSHA). No excavation rule of their own on the list (agency pages, not each code read line by line), so 5 ft: Hawaii, North Carolina, Virginia. Differ, each has its own card: Washington, California, Michigan, Maryland, South Carolina, Oregon. Not checked: Iowa, Vermont, Wyoming: federal 5 ft is the floor; ask the state plan.
source: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1); osha.gov/stateplans; AZ R20-5-601; UT R614-1-4; NM 11.5.3.9 NMAC; KY 803 KAR 2:415; 620 IAC 1-1-30 (54 FR); MNOSHA trenching fact sheet; checked 2026-11-20
note: Supersedes plan-trench-depth-1 (same ord). Takes the trench facts of sp-in-trench-1 and sp-mn-trench-1 (both retired).

title: Washington trench protection starts at 4 feet (stricter than federal 5 ft); walkway guardrails at 4 ft
topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
text: Washington (L&I, DOSH) requires a protective system for each employee in an excavation unless it is made entirely in stable rock, or it is "less than 4 feet (1.22m) in depth and examination of the ground by a competent person provides no indication of a potential cave-in" (WAC 296-155-657(1)(a)). So the depth is 4 ft, one foot shallower than the federal 5 ft (29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)). The 2 ft rules match federal: dig no more than two feet below the bottom of a support system or a shield, and only if it is designed for the full depth and no soil is being lost (657(5)(b), (7)(b)). An engineer designs slopes over 20 ft. Guardrails are required "where walkways are four feet or more above lower levels" (296-155-655(12)); federal uses 6 ft (1926.651(l)). Utilities are located before opening the excavation and found exactly by safe means as digging gets close (655(2)). Same numbers as federal: a way out within 25 ft at 4 ft deep (655(3)(b)), air testing over 4 ft (655(7)(a)(i)), equipment 2 ft from the edge (655(10)(b)), daily inspections and after every rainstorm (655(11)(a)).
edition: WAC 296-155-657, WSR 16-09-085, effective 5/20/2016; WAC 296-155-655 as amended eff. June 1, 2026
note: Takes in sp-wa-trench-other-1 (retired). The Table N-1 sentence moved to sp-wa-trench-slope-1, which already says it in full.

title: California trench protection depth (5 ft, same as federal) and the Cal/OSHA excavation permit (8 CCR 341)
topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
text: California (Cal/OSHA) requires a protective system unless the excavation is entirely in stable rock, or under 5 feet with no sign of a potential cave-in on a competent person's examination (8 CCR 1541.1(a)(1)): the same 5 ft test as federal, with the same slopes (1541.1 Appendix B). What California adds is a permit: 8 CCR 1539 sends excavation permits to 8 CCR 341, which requires a Cal/OSHA permit before building a trench or excavation 5 ft or deeper into which any person is required to descend (341(d)(5)(A)). It is an annual permit or a one-job project permit from the district office (application and fee, 341.1); an annual holder notifies the Division before each new site. Exempt (341(e)): government bodies, PUC-regulated utilities, emergency repair of underground facilities, excavations nobody has to enter, graves and pools. Greenbook 306-3.1 repeats the requirement. Keep the permit number with the job paperwork; the permit does not replace the competent person or the protective system. Shields: dig no more than 2 ft below the bottom of the support (1541.1(e)(2)(A)).
edition: Title 8 as posted on dir.ca.gov, read 2026-11-20
note: Takes in ca-cal-osha-trench-and-confined-1 and cal-1 (both retired: the same permit).

title: California trench rules that match federal (ladders, air, spoil, inspections) and the crossing rule (Title 8 Article 6)
topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
text: California's excavation standard is Title 8 Construction Safety Orders Article 6: 1539 (permits), 1540 (definitions), 1541 (general requirements) and 1541.1 (protective systems, Appendices A to F matching the federal ones; appendix options to 20 ft, an engineer beyond). It keeps the federal numbers: a stairway, ladder or ramp in trenches 4 feet or deeper within 25 feet of lateral travel (1541(c)(2)); air testing before entry deeper than 4 feet where a hazard could exist, limits 19.5 percent oxygen and 20 percent of the LFL (1541(g)(1)(A)); spoil and equipment at least 2 feet from the edge (1541(j)(2)); daily competent-person inspections before work, as needed and after rain (1541(k)(1)). Crossings differ: walkways or bridges with standard guardrails where people or equipment cross excavations more than 6 feet deep and wider than 30 inches (1541(l)(1)); remote excavations, wells, pits and shafts barricaded or covered (1541(l)(2)). The federal crossing rule has no width (29 CFR 1926.651(l)). The 5 ft permit is in section 341.
edition: Title 8 as posted on dir.ca.gov, read 2026-11-20
note: Takes in ca-cal-osha-trench-and-confined-2 (retired). Its 1541(b) one-call sentence is in sp-ca-trench-dig-1.

title: Minnesota confined space in construction: the federal rule (old state rule repealed)
text: Minnesota (MNOSHA) uses the federal confined space in construction rule, 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA: the old state construction rule, Minn. R. 5207.0300 to 5207.0304, is marked repealed (42 SR 1015; read 2026-11-19). MNOSHA's page of differences from federal OSHA lists nothing for confined space or excavation. Trenches in this state follow the federal excavation rule, 29 CFR 1926.651 and 1926.652: protection from 5 ft, or shallower when a competent person sees signs of a possible cave-in; MNOSHA's trenching fact sheet states no state difference (read by an earlier check on 2026-11-20). Any state heat rule was not read; it is not confirmed here.
source: Minn. R. 5207.0300-.0304 (repealed, 42 SR 1015); MNOSHA differences page; MNOSHA trenching fact sheet; 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA, 1926.651-652
note: New id in the ord of sp-mn-trench-1. The trench fact also sits in osha-pl-trench-states-2. "Injury reporting times not read" dropped: sp-mn-report-1 now has them.

title: California 811: the fine for digging without calling 811, and who enforces (Gov Code 4216.6, Dig Safe Board)
text: California fines for breaking the dig law (Gov. Code 4216.6(a)): a negligent violation, up to $10,000; a knowing and willful violation, up to $50,000; a knowing and willful violation that damages a gas or hazardous liquid line and lets flammable, toxic or corrosive gas or liquid escape, up to $100,000. Who enforces (4216.6(c) to (e)): the Contractors State License Board for licensed contractors (a license can be on the line); the Public Utilities Commission for gas, electric and water corporations; the State Fire Marshal for hazardous liquid pipeline operators; local boards for local agencies; and, since July 1, 2020, the Underground Facilities Safe Excavation Board (the Dig Safe Board, under the Office of the State Fire Marshal) for everyone else. The Board also investigates damages and near misses reported to it and recommends. The Attorney General or a district attorney can also sue. Repair costs and injury claims are separate. Typical: no valid ticket, digging before every operator has responded, machine digging in the tolerance zone, no delineation, not reporting damage. Keep the ticket number on the daily report, photos of the marks, and a record of hand-dug potholes.
note: Merges dig-ca-penalties-1 (this ord) and ca-dig-alert-4216-9 (retired): the same section said twice.

title: 811 wait before digging, by state: does my state use 2 working days, 48 hours, 72 hours or 3 days?
topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
text: There is no federal 811 wait time, ticket life or tolerance zone: each state's one-call law sets its own numbers. The federal floor everywhere is 49 CFR 196 for digging near pipelines: use one-call first, wait for the marks, dig with care, report damage, call 911 for a release. Wait after the call, from each state's card (use only the job state's line; the state card has the exact counting rule). 2 working or business days: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Missouri, Nebraska (app table, not re-read), Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Oregon, Washington, Wyoming. 48 hours, weekends and holidays not counted: Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Virginia, West Virginia. 72 hours: Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Vermont. 3 working or business days: Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Wisconsin. 96 hours: District of Columbia. 5 working days: Hawaii. Not confirmed: Mississippi, Montana.
source: Each state's dig-<state> card in this library (state one-call laws and 811 center handbooks, read 2026-11-20); 49 CFR 196.103-196.109
edition: State laws as read 2026-11-20; 49 CFR 196 current to Oct 22, 2026

title: 811 ticket life by state: how long is a locate ticket good for in my state?
topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
text: There is no federal 811 wait time, ticket life or tolerance zone: each state's one-call law sets its own numbers. The federal floor everywhere is 49 CFR 196 for digging near pipelines: use one-call first, wait for the marks, dig with care, report damage, call 911 for a release. Ticket life, from each state's card (use only the job state's line; days are calendar, working or business days as its card says). 14 days: Minnesota, Oklahoma, Texas (working days). 15: Arizona, District of Columbia, New Mexico, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia. 20: Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi. 21: Kentucky, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota, Utah. 25: Iowa, Illinois. 28: California, Hawaii, Nevada, North Carolina. 30: Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Oregon, Vermont, Connecticut (app table, not confirmed). 4 weeks: Idaho. 45: New Jersey (business days), Washington. 60: Maine. 12 business days: Delaware, Maryland. Each 14 business days: Wyoming. No set expiry: Alaska, New York, Rhode Island (while marks are kept up), Wisconsin, Ohio (none given, not confirmed). Not confirmed: Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Pennsylvania, West Virginia.
source: Each state's dig-<state> card in this library (state one-call laws and 811 center handbooks, read 2026-11-20); 49 CFR 196.103-196.109
edition: State laws as read 2026-11-20; 49 CFR 196 current to Oct 22, 2026

title: 811 tolerance zone (hand-dig zone) by state: 18 inches or 24 inches in my state?
topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
text: There is no federal 811 wait time, ticket life or tolerance zone: each state's one-call law sets its own numbers. The federal floor everywhere is 49 CFR 196 for digging near pipelines: use one-call first, wait for the marks, dig with care, report damage, call 911 for a release. Tolerance zone, from each state's card (use only the job state's line; measured from the mark, the edge or plus the line's width as its card says). 18 inches: Alabama (from 2027), Colorado, District of Columbia, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland (not re-read), Massachusetts, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Dakota, Vermont, Wisconsin, Texas (pipelines, plus half the diameter). 24 inches or 2 feet: Alaska, Arizona, California, Delaware, Florida, Idaho, Minnesota, Nevada, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, Utah, Washington, Wyoming; Kansas, New Jersey, Tennessee, Virginia (in the statute, not re-read). 48 inch caution zone: Michigan. Not confirmed: Arkansas, Connecticut, Hawaii, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, Montana, West Virginia.
